title: Lindsey Graham, the Senate's Loudest Voice on Iran and India, Dies at 71. His Empty Chair Changes the Calculus for Both.
excerpt: The South Carolina senator — Budget Committee chairman, immigration deal-maker, and the man who pressed Trump hardest on the Iran war now shaping life for nine million Indians in the Gulf — died of cardiac arrest Saturday night, a day after meeting Zelensky in Kyiv.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Lindsey Graham, influential senator, died at 71 from cardiac arrest.
  • His death impacts immigration policy for millions of Indians in the Gulf.
  • Graham was a key advocate for US military action against Iran.
  • His absence narrows the Republican Senate majority to 52-47.
  • Graham's successor will inherit crucial committee positions and responsibilities.
Lindsey Olin Graham, the Republican senator from South Carolina who spent two decades pressing Washington to project American military power across the globe and a lifetime navigating the fault lines of immigration policy, died on Saturday evening at his home on Capitol Hill. He was 71. His office said he died after a "brief and sudden illness." Emergency responders were called to his address for a cardiac arrest, according to police scanner traffic reviewed by *The Wall Street Journal*. He had been in Kyiv the day before, meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on what was his tenth trip to the country since Russia's invasion. "He was one of the greatest people and Senators I have ever known," President Trump posted early Sunday. Senate Majority Leader John Thune said his heart was heavy. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called Graham Israel's greatest friend in the Senate. South Carolina Governor Henry McMaster called him "irreplaceable." For the Indian diaspora in America and the millions of Indians navigating the Gulf's escalating crisis, Graham's death removes a senator whose positions — on immigration, on India's strategic partnership with Washington, on the Iran war — touched their lives in ways most never tracked. ## The Immigration Record Graham sat on the Senate Judiciary Committee, the body through which every major piece of immigration legislation passes. In 2013, he was one of the architects of the bipartisan "Gang of Eight" immigration reform bill — a sweeping overhaul that passed the Senate but died in the House. That bill would have created pathways affecting hundreds of thousands of Indian nationals in the green card backlog. His record was complicated. He participated in hearings on L-1 visa abuse by Indian outsourcing firms including Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, and Infosys, where committee members questioned whether the programme was being used to undercut American wages. He later shifted rightward on immigration during Trump's rise, aligning with tougher enforcement and border security measures. ![Capitol Hill — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/20/8th_Street_SE_sidewalk_scene.jpg/3840px-8th_Street_SE_sidewalk_scene.jpg) > **"In 2013, he was one of the architects of the bipartisan "Gang of Eight" immigration reform bill — a sweeping overhaul that passed the Senate but died in the House."** But Graham remained, by Republican standards, relatively open to legal immigration reform. His absence from the Judiciary Committee removes a senator who understood the granular mechanics of visa policy — at a moment when the Trump administration is simultaneously rewriting H-1B fee structures, launching fraud investigations targeting Indian workers, and tightening H-4 EAD rules. ## The Iran War and Nine Million Indians Graham was among the Senate's loudest advocates for military action against Iran and one of the key voices who pressed Trump to strike. He cheered the decision and remained a prominent supporter of the US-Israeli campaign against the Iranian regime. That campaign has now produced the crisis dominating Indian foreign policy: the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the trapping of Indian seafarers in the Persian Gulf, and the energy shock rippling through an economy that imports 85 percent of its crude oil. Nine million Indians live and work in Gulf states now caught in the conflict's widening arc. As chairman of the Senate Budget Committee, Graham controlled the purse strings for the very defence spending that funds the war he championed. His replacement — to be appointed by Governor McMaster — will inherit that chairmanship at a moment when the war's costs are ballooning and its consequences for energy markets are acute. ## The India-US Defence Corridor Graham was a consistent advocate of the US-India strategic partnership, particularly on defence cooperation. His hawkish posture on the Indo-Pacific aligned with India's own strategic interests in countering China. He supported defence sales to India and backed the kind of interoperability agreements — LEMOA, COMCASA, BECA — that have deepened military ties over the past decade.

The BrahMos missile deal India just signed with Indonesia, the uranium agreement sealed with Australia during Modi's visit, and the broader Indo-Pacific arms architecture all sit within a strategic framework that senators like Graham actively championed on the American side. ## What Happens Now With Graham's death, the Republican Senate majority narrows to 52-47. Combined with Senator Mitch McConnell's health-related absence, the GOP's effective working majority is thinner than it has been since the party retook the chamber. Governor McMaster will appoint a successor under South Carolina law. That appointee will inherit Graham's Budget Committee chairmanship and his seats on the Judiciary, Appropriations, and Environment committees. The appointment carries no requirement for a special election. Graham had won a Republican primary last month and was favoured to win re-election in November. His successor will serve until the next election and will face an electorate that has not sent a Democrat to the Senate from South Carolina since 2005. For the Indian-American community — now the second-largest immigrant group in the United States — Graham's death reshapes the Senate landscape on immigration at a uniquely volatile moment. The $100,000 H-1B fee has been struck down by a federal judge. The administration's fraud probe is escalating. The green card backlog remains north of a million applicants, overwhelmingly Indian nationals.

The senator who understood all of these levers, who sat in the rooms where they were pulled, is gone. What his successor does with the same levers will matter to every Indian family waiting in that line. *Sources: Wall Street Journal, Reuters, The Sun, C-SPAN Congressional Records, Senate Judiciary Committee testimony archives*
